1.observations: No previous sales or profit data was provided, and the market data section is empty. Known facts: unit cost is 1.00, and no customer would pay more than 4.51. The feasible price range is therefore 1.00 to 4.51, and any price at or below 1.00 yields no profit.
1.plans: 1) Launch at 2.75 as a baseline. If customer willingness to pay is roughly uniform on [0, 4.51], this maximizes expected profit (the midpoint of cost and maximum WTP), so it is a principled starting point. 2) Once at least a few sales periods of data exist, compare profit per visitor (or per period) at 2.25, 2.75, 3.25, and 3.75. 3) Estimate demand elasticity from the volume response at each price and fit a simple demand curve (for example, linear in price) to locate the profit-maximizing price. 4) Refine within 0.25 of the best-performing price. 5) Re-check periodically for demand shifts, since a price that is optimal now may drift. Do not go above 4.51, since no customer would pay that.
1.insights: With no demand data, the choice rests on a standard assumption: if willingness to pay is spread evenly from 0 to the 4.51 cap, expected profit P(p) = (p - 1)(1 - p/4.51) peaks at p ≈ 2.755. Real markets are rarely uniform, so this is only a prior to be tested. Profit is highly sensitive to price near the cost floor: prices just above 1.00 may sell many units but earn tiny margins, while prices near 4.51 earn large margins on very few sales. The midpoint is a robust starting point that avoids both extremes.
